                   SUPPLEMENTAL COMMENTS OF THE
           SOUTHWEST POWER POOL TRANSMISSION OWNER GROUP

       The Southwest Power Pool Transmission Owner Group (SPP TO Group) 1 respectfully

submits the following supplemental comments to the Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking

(ANOPR) to memorialize in the record recent developments pertinent to this proceeding.

Specifically, the SPP TO Group has attached, as Attachments A and B respectively, the

Commission’s orders accepting the High Impact Large Load (HILL) 2 and Consolidated Planning

Process (CPP) 3 reforms recently filed by Southwest Power Pool Inc. (SPP). Those orders provide

convincing support for the SPP TO Group’s position that the Commission should avoid issuing an

overly prescriptive rule, but should instead provide broad latitude for transmission providers and

their stakeholders to develop their own solutions to the challenges posed by large load

interconnections.




1

Central, Inc., Evergy Metro, Inc., Evergy Missouri West, Inc., Oklahoma Gas and Electric
Company, and Xcel Energy Services Inc. on behalf of Southwestern Public Service Company.

           To underscore this point, the SPP TO Group explains how a series of integrated SPP market

reforms already engage with each of the fourteen ANOPR principles to accomplish the

Administration’s goals in a manner that is legally durable and overwhelmingly supported by SPP

stakeholders. Those reforms often conform to the ANOPR’s recommendations, but sometimes

achieve the Administration’s intent through alternative means. The Commission has already

accepted CPP and HILL, while the Commission continues to examine SPP’s pending Conditional

High Impact Large Load Service (CHILLS) proposal. 4

          At bottom, the SPP TO Group believes that it is less “necessary to standardize

interconnection procedures,” 5 than it is to accomplish the ANOPR’s fundamental objective “to

ensure the timely and orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.” 6

Standardization is merely a tool to achieve that end; it is not an end in itself. A final rule in this

proceeding should not undermine the extraordinary progress the SPP region has made by

disturbing the carefully balanced consensus reforms that SPP, its public and investor-owned Load

Serving Entities, and state regulators have collaborated to develop.

I.        THE HILL AND CPP REFORMS SHOW THE NEED FOR REGIONAL

 II.      SPP HAS ALREADY ADDRESSED THE ANOPR PRINCIPLES

         The ANOPR states fourteen principles the Administration proposed “to ensure the timely

and orderly interconnection of large loads to the transmission system.” 18 Below, the SPP TO

Group explains how SPP engaged with each of those principles through CPP, HILL, and its

pending CHILLS reform. Those reforms often conform to the ANOPR’s recommendations, but

sometimes achieve the Administration’s intent through alternative means. SPP has good reasons

for those deliberate departures, 19 which the SPP TO Group believes will be more effective in the

SPP region than the standardized recommendations in the ANOPR.

        A.     Principle 1

         The ANOPR first proposes that “to avoid even arguably affecting the States’ jurisdiction

over generation facilities, facilities used in local distribution or only for the transmission of electric

energy in intrastate commerce, or transmissions consumed by the transmitter,” the Commission’s

jurisdiction be “limited to interconnections directly to transmission facilities, consistent with the

Commission’s seven-factor test.” 20

         Neither the CPP nor the HILL reforms encroach on state jurisdiction. In particular, CPP

unified the interconnection of load and generation in one process with the unanimous support of

its stakeholders, including the states in its region. SPP’s Regional State Committee—comprised

of retail regulatory commissioners from Arkansas, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri,

Straying from the 20 MW threshold definition of “large load” makes sense in SPP due to the

prevalence of 69 kV lines in the Eastern Interconnection portion of SPP’s region and because “the

size of the load may impact SPP’s transmission system differently at different voltage levels.” 26

While a 20 MW threshold may work for other regions, it would not work for SPP. However,

transmission providers outside of SPP should be left to define “large loads” as they see fit with

their stakeholders and according to their region’s unique circumstances. The Commission need

not dictate what the limit is, although it should direct all transmission providers to designate and

justify an appropriate threshold.

         H.     Principle 8

         The ANOPR proposes that “load and hybrid facilities should be responsible for 100% of

           Because SPP is primarily served by vertically integrated utilities and not Independent

Power Producers (IPPs), Principle 10 is not relevant to SPP. Unlike IPPs, vertically integrated

utilities are public utilities required to serve all of their customers. They do not have a reason—

nor the ability—to divert their generation away from their customers. In other regions where that

is an issue, the relevant transmission providers have already addressed it through their existing

tariffs, as the SPP TO Group explained in its initial comments. 56 Those regional variations

illustrate why the Commission should avoid a broad, overly prescriptive rule.

         K.     Principle 11

          The ANOPR proposes that “utilities serving large loads, including those at hybrid facilities,

should be responsible for transmission service based on their withdrawal rights, as that value

amount reflects the quantity of capacity and energy that will be transmitted across the transmission

system to the load.” 57 To the extent that “their withdrawal rights” refers to the withdrawal from

the transmission system by the load, the HILL reform already adopts that framework. The HILL

reform treats large loads and co-located generation as distinct for tariff and metering purposes and

assesses transmission service on the load’s gross withdrawals, not net of on-site generation at the

same bus. 58

 III.    CONCLUSION

        For the reasons set forth above, the SPP TO Group respectfully requests that the

ROSNER, Commissioner, concurring:

        Today’s order accepts SPP’s proposal to establish new study processes for new
High Impact Large Loads (HILLs) and associated generation through the High Impact
Large Load Generation Assessment (HILLGA). Together, these processes will enable
SPP to efficiently identify new large loads, expedite the interconnection of new
generation needed to serve them, and protect the reliability of the bulk power system.
The proposal also encourages “bring-your-own-new-generation” solutions in SPP, which
will enable rapid interconnection of new large loads without raising costs or threatening
electric reliability for other customers. I concur to highlight SPP’s pragmatic steps to
support economic growth in its footprint and call on other transmission providers across
the country to consider similar proposals through FPA section 205 filings.
        The HILLs and HILLGA processes work together to pair shovel-ready generation
with large loads and allow them to interconnect to the grid in less than half the time
typically required for generators to clear SPP’s generator interconnection queue. The
secret sauce behind SPP’s proposal is Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service
(LLRIS), a new interconnection service that limits the amount of power a generator can
put on the SPP grid to the forecasted hourly load of the nearby large load it serves.
Because the generator’s output is matched to the large load’s demand, the impacts of
adding load and generation to the transmission system effectively cancel each other out,
which minimizes the need for time-consuming transmission upgrades. SPP’s proposal is
grounded in physics, takes a harder look at reliability impacts of large loads on the grid
than current practice requires, and unlocks large load opportunities while protecting other
customers from rising bills.
       There are also clear parallels between SPP’s approach in its HILLs and HILLGA
processes and the new transmission services the Commission recently directed PJM to
create for load co-located with generation. 1 While the mechanics of these approaches are
distinct between the different regions, the practical outcome is similar: they both enable
new generation needed to serve new large loads to connect to the grid faster and at lower

                             i.     GRID-C Mechanism

        We find that SPP’s proposed GRID-C mechanism is just and reasonable and not
unduly discriminatory or preferential. SPP’s proposed CPP framework presents a novel
approach where SPP, as the transmission provider, will analyze the projected needs of
future interconnection customers, incorporate that analysis into its regional transmission
planning process, and then allocate a share of the costs of the transmission upgrades
identified in that planning process to interconnection customers. Under this framework,
unlike under typical generator interconnection procedures where the Commission has
applied the “but for” principle, the specific interconnection customers and exact network
upgrades needed to effectuate their interconnection are not definitively known before the
CPP-20 portfolio is identified and the GRID-C rate is calculated. In that regard, we find
that SPP’s CPP proposal is more akin to a transmission planning process that identifies
effective regional transmission solutions to address transmission needs than to a
traditional, reactive generator interconnection process that identifies only those network
upgrades needed to accommodate a specific interconnection request or cluster of
interconnection requests. 200 As such, we apply the Commission’s “beneficiary pays”
application of the cost causation principle to the proposed GRID-C mechanism to
determine whether it is just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.

       Under Commission precedent, costs must be allocated according to the cost
causation principle, which requires that “all approved rates reflect to some degree the
costs actually caused by the customer who must pay them.” 201 Courts have further
explained that, to “the extent that a utility benefits from the costs of new facilities, it may
be said to have ‘caused’ a part of those costs to be incurred, as without the expectation of
its contributions the facilities might not have been built, or might have been delayed.” 202
As a result, a cost allocation method can satisfy the cost causation principle if the
Commission “has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are at
